whyThisMatters: An unreachable supervisor, a detention-fee demand, or an urgent cargo redirect all put the same pressure on Operations: act now, verify later. But a permit, a payment, or a vessel's course are exactly the kind of decisions that need the normal process followed, especially when someone is pushing you to skip it.
rememberThis: The one line to take from this whole month: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT. "Just this once" is never a real exception to a safety sign-off, a payment process, or a charter instruction — verify through your own known channel before you act, no matter who is asking.

discussionPrompts: Ask what the team's actual process is when a laptop goes missing — does everyone know to report immediately rather than search for it first?
For the permit sign-off case, ask why an unreachable supervisor plus urgency is the pattern to catch, not a reason to proceed.
For the ransomware case, ask if everyone actually knows how to disconnect their own machine from the network quickly.
For the new crew-change and weather-routing cases, ask why replying to the sender to ask for confirmation doesn't actually verify anything.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get the permit sign-off and charter redirect cases wrong, treating a senior title or a claimed emergency as enough reason to skip the normal process. The habit to build is the same one every case points to: verify through your own known channel — your own PSC liaison, port agent, or the agreed charter-desk process — before you skip a step, redirect anything, or pay a fee.

cases.title: Your Work Laptop Went Missing
cases.scenario: You just finished a vessel visit at the port. You travelled back on the launch, and when you get to the jetty you realise your work laptop is gone — it was in your bag during the transfer.

decisions.prompt: You just noticed it is gone. What do you do first?

options.text: Go back to the jetty and the launch to search for it yourself
options.feedback: Every minute you spend searching is a minute the IT Service Desk is not locking your accounts or wiping the device. Speed matters more than searching.

options.text: Report it to the IT Service Desk and your manager immediately
options.feedback: Correct. Fast reporting lets the IT Service Desk act while there is still time to lock things.

cases.debrief: A missing device with company access is a race against time. STOP trying to find it yourself. REPORT right away to the IT Service Desk and your manager with what you know. Check that the next steps happened, like locking the device remotely and changing your password.

cases.title: Skip the Permit Sign-Off?
cases.scenario: You get a Teams message — Teams is the work chat app — from someone you do not recognise. No photo, no chat history. They say the site supervisor cannot be reached. They ask you to skip the permit-to-work sign-off — the signed safety approval before hot work or enclosed-space entry — "just this once" so the schedule does not slip.

decisions.prompt: What is the warning sign here?

options.text: It is fine — schedules matter, and you can sort out the paperwork later
options.feedback: Treating a safety sign-off as paperwork you can “sort out later” is exactly the mistake this message is engineered to cause — the permit exists precisely for situations like this.

options.text: Someone you cannot verify is pressuring you to skip a safety approval, using urgency and "the boss is unreachable" as the excuse
options.feedback: Correct. An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a required safety approval because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag — the same trick as a fake-boss email asking for a wire transfer, just aimed at a safety step instead of money.

options.text: It is a normal, routine reminder about the schedule
options.feedback: This is not routine — an unrecognised sender asking you to bypass a signed safety approval is never a normal reminder, no matter how it is phrased.

options.text: It is expected — supervisors often message from other accounts
options.feedback: Real supervisors don’t ask you to bypass safety sign-offs from an unrecognised account with no history — that pattern is the red flag, not something to wave away as normal account-switching.

cases.debrief: An unverified sender plus time pressure plus a request to skip a normal check is the same pattern as a fake-boss scam — just aimed at a safety process instead of a payment.

cases.title: Your Screen Just Locked
cases.scenario: A message covers your office computer screen. It says your files are locked and you must pay to get them back. A countdown timer is running. This is ransomware — harmful software that locks your files until you pay.

options.text: Try to pay quickly before the timer runs out
options.feedback: Paying does not guarantee you get your files back. It also funds the next attack. And you skip reporting, which is what the IT Service Desk needs most.

options.text: Disconnect the computer from the network right away (unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi) and leave it alone
options.feedback: Right idea. Disconnecting quickly can stop it from spreading to other computers before the IT Service Desk steps in.

options.text: Post about it in the team chat to warn others
options.feedback: This is understandable, but it is not the fastest way to contain it. It can also cause panic before the IT Service Desk knows how far it has spread.

cases.debrief: Ransomware — harmful software that locks your files for payment — wants you to panic and pay. STOP by disconnecting the computer from the network right away (unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi). Do not try to pay or fix it yourself. REPORT fast to the IT Service Desk so they can stop it from reaching other systems.

cases.title: The Detention Fee Demand
cases.scenario: An email claiming to be a Port Authority Notice says MV Horizon has an unpaid deficiency fee on record and must pay immediately via the account provided to avoid detention.

options.text: Pay the fee immediately to avoid the vessel being detained
options.feedback: Paying a fee straight from an unverified email, with a detention threat attached, is exactly how this authority-impersonation scam is designed to work.

options.text: Reply to the email asking for more documentation of the deficiency
options.feedback: A fake sender can produce plausible-looking documentation — this does not confirm the request came through a genuine channel.

options.text: Check with your own PSC liaison and port agent through their known channels before considering any payment
options.feedback: Correct. Real Port State Control deficiencies and any fees go through your own company's documented channels — verifying there, not with the email itself, confirms whether anything is actually owed.

cases.debrief: A detention threat is designed to force a fast payment without verification. STOP before paying anything. VERIFY through your own PSC liaison and port agent. REPORT the email regardless of what you find.

cases.title: The Urgent Cargo Redirect Instruction
cases.scenario: An email that looks like it's from the charterer's operations desk says a commercial emergency requires you to redirect the vessel's discharge port and cargo instructions immediately — with no signed addendum, just the email itself.

options.text: Redirect the vessel as instructed, since commercial emergencies can move fast
options.feedback: Acting on a major operational change from an email alone, with no signed addendum, is exactly the gap this kind of Business Email Compromise attempt is designed to exploit.

options.text: Reply asking the charterer to confirm the emergency before redirecting
options.feedback: A fake sender can simply confirm whatever you ask — this doesn't verify the request came through the real charter-desk process.

options.text: Do not redirect anything without a signed addendum through the agreed charter-desk process, and verify with the charterer directly
options.feedback: Correct. A change as significant as redirecting a vessel always requires a signed addendum through the agreed process — verifying directly with the charterer, not just replying to the email, confirms whether it's genuine.

cases.debrief: An instruction to redirect the vessel based on an email alone, with no signed addendum, is the red flag. STOP before acting on it. VERIFY through the agreed charter-desk process. REPORT the email regardless of the outcome.

cases.title: The Crew Change Rebooking Fee
cases.scenario: An email claiming to be from your manning agency contact says the crew's flight was cancelled, and a rebooking fee must be paid today to a newly provided account to keep the crew change on schedule.

options.text: Pay the rebooking fee today to the account provided, since the crew change date is fixed
options.feedback: Paying a fee to a newly provided account on a message alone is exactly the advance-fee pattern this scam relies on — a fixed date is the pressure, not a reason to skip verification.

options.text: Ask the sender for proof of the flight cancellation before paying
options.feedback: A fake sender can produce a convincing-looking cancellation notice — that doesn't confirm the request or the new account are genuine.

options.text: Contact the manning agency directly through their known contact to confirm before paying anything
options.feedback: Correct. Manning agencies invoice through the agreed process — verifying directly with your known contact, not the email itself, is what actually confirms whether anything changed.

cases.debrief: A cancelled flight paired with a new payment account is a classic advance-fee scam. STOP before paying. VERIFY with the manning agency's known contact. REPORT the email regardless of what you find.

cases.title: The Urgent Routing Change
cases.scenario: An email that looks like it's from your weather-routing service arrives with an attachment recommending an immediate, costly course change to avoid bad weather — but it didn't come through the routing portal you normally use.

options.text: Open the attachment and action the course change immediately, since weather routing can't wait
options.feedback: Opening an unexpected attachment and acting on a routing change from outside your normal process is exactly the gap this kind of scam is built to exploit.

options.text: Reply to the email asking the routing service to confirm the recommendation
options.feedback: A fake sender can simply confirm whatever you ask — this doesn't verify the message came through your actual routing provider.

options.text: Check the recommendation directly through your routing provider's own portal before changing course
options.feedback: Correct. A genuine routing change is always available through the provider's own portal — confirming there, not through the email or its attachment, is what actually verifies it.

cases.debrief: An urgent routing change that bypasses the portal you normally use is the red flag, regardless of how convincing the weather claim sounds. STOP before changing course. VERIFY through your routing provider's own portal. REPORT the email regardless of what you find.
